title: Care for animals
hook: Jewish law forbids causing animals needless suffering

segments.voice: Yesterday, pareve: neither meat nor milk, and a kitchen with two sides. Your line was some things stay apart. Today, the animals themselves. Day one hundred forty-seven.

The Talmud tells a story about Rabbi Judah the Prince, the sage tradition credits with compiling the Mishnah. One day a calf was being led to slaughter. It broke away, ran to him, hid its head in his clothes, and cried. And the rabbi said to it: go. This is what you were created for. The story says that because he showed no pity, he suffered years of illness. Then one day his housekeeper was sweeping out some baby weasels, and he stopped her.
screen: `A CALF RUNS TO THE RABBI.` → `GO, THIS IS WHAT YOU'RE FOR.` → `THEN, THE BABY WEASELS.`

segments.voice: He told her to leave them alone, quoting a psalm: "His tender mercies are over all His works." And the Talmud says: because he showed mercy, his suffering ended. That story sits at the heart of a principle in Jewish law called tza'ar ba'alei chayim, the suffering of living creatures. It means you may not cause an animal needless pain. The Talmud debates whether this rule comes straight from the Torah or from the rabbis, and later authorities argue both ways. Where would you find it? Look at how many of the Torah's laws protect animals. If you see even your enemy's donkey collapsed under its load, the Torah says: "thou shalt surely release it with him." Help him, enemy or not, for the animal's sake. "Thou shalt not muzzle the ox when he treadeth out the corn": let a working animal eat from what it's working on. On Shabbat, your ox and donkey rest too. If you take eggs from a nest, first send the mother bird away. The Talmud even derives a rule about mealtime from a verse in the Shema, which says God will give grass for your cattle, and then says you'll eat and be satisfied. Cattle first, then you. So Jewish law says to feed your animals before you sit down to eat. This connects back to kosher food too: the traditional method of slaughter, shechita, is meant to be a single swift cut, and an animal that's badly injured or diseased isn't kosher. Look at our week: the head, the strap like a ring, who wears them, what kosher means, which animals, meat and milk, and now the animals' own suffering.
screen: `OVER ALL HIS WORKS.` · `NO NEEDLESS SUFFERING.` · `RELEASE THE DONKEY, EVEN AN ENEMY'S.` · `FEED YOUR ANIMALS FIRST.` · then, large: `HIS TENDER MERCIES ARE OVER ALL.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: be gentle with an animal today. A pet, a bird at the window, an insect you'd usually swat, a dog on the sidewalk. For now, settle, and breathe. Picture that animal. Notice that it has a body like yours: it gets hungry, tired, scared. Let yourself feel that for a moment. Then decide on one small kindness you can offer. Fresh water, a gentle hand, or simply letting something go out the window instead of squashing it. The bell holds the time.
Ba'alei chayim. Living creatures, the Hebrew phrase at the heart of the Jewish principle that you may not cause an animal needless pain.
Your line: animals feel too. If you have an animal in your care, feed it before you feed yourself today. Day one hundred forty-seven.

howItsDone: Jewish law forbids causing animals needless suffering; many Jews feed their animals before eating themselves, let working animals rest on Shabbat, and expect kosher slaughter to be a single swift cut.

what it means: a principle of Jewish law, built from many Torah commands, forbidding needless pain to any animal.
what a scholar hears: Bava Metzia 32b debates whether it's biblical; Bava Metzia 85a tells the calf and the weasels; Berakhot 40a derives feeding animals first from Deuteronomy 11:15.

notes: Confirm JPS 1917 wording of Psalms 145:9, Exodus 23:5 and Deuteronomy 25:4.
Rabbi Judah and the calf / weasels: Bava Metzia 85a; paraphrased. Confirm the thirteen years of suffering is left unstated.
Biblical vs. rabbinic status of tza'ar ba'alei chayim: Bava Metzia 32b; 'many authorities say from the Torah' (e.g. Maimonides, Shulchan Aruch HaRav). Confirm.
Feeding animals first: Berakhot 40a from Deuteronomy 11:15; confirm.
